parallel.requirements: The parallel run recognized the Python-to-Node migration, ESM-only .mjs files, manual argparse-compatible parsing, exact print/error behavior, no external modules, and output under /output.
parallel.plan_and_ownership: The parent retained the main implementation path while also spawning one child to probe and implement the same test8 behavior, creating overlapping ownership of the entrypoint and helper modules.
parallel.implementation: Both parent and child implemented CLI parsing, Python-like JSON errors, a Draft7 type-checker shim, and /output/test8.mjs with helper modules, but the parent's later tree became the delivered artifact.
parallel.integration_and_delivery: The parent wrote a complete /output tree after the child had already written one, did not merge a returned child result, interrupted the child, and delivered its own files.
parallel.verification: The parent ran representative executable and Node comparisons for help text, required arguments, known and unknown types, malformed JSON, and invalid schema roots, while the child was also still running verification when stopped.
parallel.unfinished_or_incorrect: The final response acknowledged a remaining mismatch on the bundled executable's PyInstaller trailer, and official evaluation failed 156 of 157 samples.

serial.requirements: The serial run recognized the same ESM, .mjs, manual CLI parsing, local-only module, black-box executable, and /output delivery constraints.
serial.plan_and_ownership: One agent owned the full pipeline: behavior probing, implementation, correction, verification, and final response, with no child delegation or parallel workspace owner split.
serial.implementation: The serial agent created a single ESM module tree for CLI parsing, Python-style errors, JSON parsing, Draft7 validator construction, type checking, and the test8.mjs entrypoint.
serial.integration_and_delivery: The serial implementation evolved in place through its own patches, including a JSON shim replacement and CLI help-token adjustment, then delivered one coherent artifact tree.
serial.verification: The serial run verified many executable-aligned cases, including help, missing arguments, unknown arguments, equals forms, duplicate flags, known and unknown types, invalid schema roots, and malformed JSON.
serial.unfinished_or_incorrect: Despite cleaner single-threaded ownership and verification, the official evaluator still marked the solution failed with 1 of 157 passing.

comparison_dimensions.difference: Parallel had coordination overhead and an unfinished child lifecycle at closure; serial had ordinary single-agent residual defects.

outcome_analysis.explanation: The current completed official evaluations are not discordant: both parallel and serial failed with 1 passed sample out of 157. The concrete task-solving difference is process-level rather than outcome-level: parallel duplicated implementation work across parent and child, overwrote the child-created entrypoint, and terminated the active child before it could return a final result, while serial kept a single owner and edited one artifact tree. These adverse parallel events do not explain a different official outcome because the serial control also failed the same number of samples.
parallel_contributors: Parent and child independently wrote /output/test8.mjs and helper modules in the shared output tree.
The parent interrupted the running child before receiving a final handoff.
serial_contributors: Serial kept behavior probing, implementation, correction, verification, and delivery in one thread.
Serial still delivered an implementation that failed the official hidden suite.
ordinary_implementation_differences: Both runs relied on local representative probes rather than exhaustive evaluator-aligned coverage of jsonschema behavior.
The parallel final response explicitly noted a PyInstaller trailer mismatch; the serial final response did not identify that gap.
outcome_analysis.causal_scope: No outcome difference; retained patterns are realized adverse parallel-side process defects, not explanations for a discordant result.

candidates.reason: An implementation owner existed: the parent implemented and delivered the final artifact, while the child also implemented overlapping code.
The issue was not an unowned integration step; the parent owned delivery and overwrote/replaced the child implementation instead of leaving integration unassigned.
The parent assembled and placed /output/test8.mjs and helpers, so final assembly had an owner even though the shared write boundary was flawed.

The parent drove the end-to-end pipeline through probing, implementation, verification, cleanup, and final response; the problem was overlapping shared-state ownership, not absence of pipeline ownership.
Both parent and child probed while implementation proceeded later, but no mandatory serial preflight gate blocked all productive work.
There was overlapped probing and later duplicate implementation, not a completed investigation-only phase that serially deferred all implementation and caused the failure.
No indispensable implementation path was starved by auxiliary allocation; the direct adverse event was conflicting writes plus later child interruption.
The parallel run spawned only one child and did not exhaust budget through excessive breadth or retries before producing a deliverable.
Although the child attempted a broad implementation, the directly evidenced boundary is parent interruption of an active child and overwrite of its deliverable, not scope size alone.
The child received the same prompt context and independently pursued executable probing plus /output delivery; the observed failure was not caused by a missing known requirement in the initial brief.
A file ownership contract was absent, but the realized event was a concrete overwrite of the entrypoint deliverable, which takes precedence over a generic interface-contract label.
No known finding is shown disappearing during transfer; the child was interrupted before a final handoff, which is a lifecycle issue.
The child did not return an oversized completed report that the parent failed to reduce; it was still running when interrupted.
There is no completed handoff consumed by the parent that described superseded state; the stale-current-file symptom arose from a live write collision.
No incompatible completed reports reached the parent for adjudication; the conflict was a concrete shared-file overwrite.
The parent did verify many whole-program cases and explicitly disclosed a remaining mismatch; the official hidden failure alone cannot establish unsupported completion under this label.
There was no replacement or retry agent repeating work without inherited checkpoint state.

taxonomy_decisions.sub_label: Wrong Start, Join, or Result Timing

candidates.reason: The parent observed the child still running after a wait timeout and explicitly interrupted it; the child trajectory then ended with turn_aborted before a final result handoff.
candidates.realized_consequence: The active child never returned a final handoff, so its in-progress verification and correction work was unavailable to the parent at closure.
candidates.near_match_reason: The missing information was caused by an explicit interrupt of a running child, not a verifier finding trapped below the parent after normal completion.

candidates.reason: No complete child candidate was waiting to be promoted; the child's candidate was in flux and had just hit a patch mismatch before interruption.
The parent verified after writing its own implementation; there is no completed child merge after integrated verification.
The child implementation was not a completed retrievable result ignored at join time; it had been overwritten and was still active when interrupted.
The child was an implementation/probing child and did not complete a concrete verifier finding; the directly observed lifecycle event is Early Child Termination.
The parent had already produced and delivered its own implementation, so the missed child result is better captured by explicit early termination, not a separate failure-takeover episode.
No completed child result was available and ignored by the parent; the child was still running.
The parent did wait to timeout, but then inspected agent status and chose to interrupt; the direct harmful boundary is the interruption, not blind waiting.
The agents did more than write different files with overlapping behavior; they wrote the same required entrypoint path, so the more specific deliverable overwrite applies.
The same-file collision was on /output/test8.mjs, the submitted entrypoint source, so Deliverable Overwrite is the canonical more specific label.
Helper modules were also affected, but the entrypoint deliverable overwrite has precedence over non-entry source overwrite for this write episode.

The child first created /output/test8.mjs and helper modules, the parent later wrote its own /output/test8.mjs and overlapping helper tree while the child was still active, and the child then could not apply a patch because the current entrypoint no longer matched its expected version.
candidates.realized_consequence: The child-created entrypoint was superseded by the parent's delivered entrypoint, and the child's later correction patch failed against the changed current file.
candidates.near_match_reason: Same-File Collision is visible, but the same file was the required executable entrypoint source, making Deliverable Overwrite the more specific canonical label.

candidates.reason: Multiple output files changed, but the specific affected required entrypoint /output/test8.mjs gives the deliverable-overwrite label precedence.
The shared workspace was unisolated, but a more specific deliverable overwrite is directly proven.
No generated fixture, cache, temporary file, tool, or auxiliary artifact from one actor was consumed by another as stable reference input.
